section.title: The Prosperity of the Wicked
section.sectionRationale: Opening Book III with Asaph's wisdom crisis over the easy, carefree prosperity of the wicked, this psalm's turning point, 'until I entered God's sanctuary, then I discerned their end,' models how nearness to God, not mere reasoning, resolves the believer's hardest doubts.
section.thesis: Watching the wicked prosper nearly toppled Asaph's faith, until entering God's presence reordered his perspective, leaving him with a confession that outlasts every earthly loss: God is the strength of his heart and his portion forever.
section.frameNote: Five movements: an opening confession and near stumble, verses 1 to 3; the prosperity of the wicked described, verses 4 to 12; the crisis and turning point in the sanctuary, verses 13 to 17; the wicked's hidden fate unveiled, verses 18 to 22; renewed nearness to God, verses 23 to 28.

verses.text: A Psalm of Asaph. Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart.
But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped.
For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
They have no struggle in their death; their bodies are well-fed.
They are free of the burdens others carry; they are not afflicted like other men.
Therefore pride is their necklace; a garment of violence covers them.
From their prosperity proceeds iniquity; the imaginations of their hearts run wild.
They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression.
They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth.
So their people return to this place and drink up waters in abundance.
The wicked say, "How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?"
Behold, these are the wicked, always carefree as they increase their wealth.
Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands.
For I am afflicted all day long and punished every morning.
If I had said, "I will speak this way," then I would have betrayed Your children.
When I tried to understand all this, it was troublesome in my sight
until I entered God's {{miqdash|sanctuary}}; then I discerned their end.
Surely You set them on {{chalaqot|slick}} ground; You cast them down into ruin.
How suddenly they are laid waste, completely swept away by terrors!
Like one waking from a dream, so You, O Lord, awaken and despise their form.
When my heart was grieved and I was pierced within,
I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You.
Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand.
You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory.
Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You.
My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
Those far from You will surely perish; You destroy all who are unfaithful to You.
But as for me, it is good to draw near to God. I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may proclaim all Your works.

miqdash.gloss: Sanctuary, holy place, the place set apart for God's presence. Asaph's crisis of faith is not resolved by more reasoning but by entering this place, where God's presence reorders how he sees the wicked's apparent success.

chalaqot.gloss: Slippery, slick places. What looked like solid ground under the wicked's feet is revealed, once seen from the sanctuary, to be treacherously unstable, a picture of security that can collapse in an instant.

basic.context: Opening Book III, this psalm of Asaph honestly confesses a near collapse of faith brought on by watching arrogant, wicked people live carefree, wealthy, and untroubled lives, until entering God's sanctuary reorders his whole perspective.
basic.hermeneutics: This is an honest wisdom psalm wrestling with the classic problem of the prosperity of the wicked; it does not deny the reality of that prosperity but resolves the crisis not through argument but through nearness to God.
basic.originalLanguages: The turning point comes when Asaph enters God's miqdash, sanctuary, verse 17, and discovers the wicked stand on chalaqot, slippery ground, verse 18, ground that looked solid but was never secure at all.
basic.typology: Asaph's confession, 'Whom have I in heaven but You,' anticipates the greater satisfaction found only in Christ, and his hope of later being 'received in glory' anticipates the believer's union with the risen Christ who has gone before to prepare a place.
basic.christ: Asaph's cry, 'God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever,' is answered fully in Christ, in whom believers are promised an inheritance that cannot perish, spoil, or fade, 1 Peter 1:4, and whose own resurrection guarantees that being 'received in glory' is no mere hope but a certainty.
basic.god: God is shown as the only true and lasting good, One who holds the psalmist's hand through confusion, guides him with counsel, and receives him in glory, even while the seemingly secure prosperity of the wicked proves to be built on nothing.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 1:4 promises an inheritance that never perishes, echoing Asaph's 'portion forever.' Philippians 3:8 counts everything as loss compared to knowing Christ, matching Asaph's 'whom have I in heaven but You.' Hebrews 12:2 shows looking to Jesus as the resolution for weary, doubting faith.
basic.oneStory: This wisdom crisis over the prosperity of the wicked, resolved only in the sanctuary of God's presence, threads into the whole Bible's story of a people learning that true and lasting good is found in God alone, a truth secured forever in Christ, our portion who never fails.

context.literary:
Psalm 73 is a story told from the far side of a crisis, and it is built as a turn. The first twelve verses set out the problem: the psalmist's slip, the ease of the ungodly, their pride and their speech. Verses 13 to 16 give the crisis, an argument that faith has been pointless that he stops just short of saying aloud. Verse 17 is the hinge, 'until I entered God's sanctuary.' Everything after verse 17 is what he sees from the new place: the end of the wicked in verses 18 to 20, his own confession in 21 to 22, and his renewed possession of God in verses 23 to 28.

The Hebrew word 'ak, usually 'surely,' opens verses 1, 13 and 18, and the three occurrences mark the psalm's three positions. In verse 1 it states the creed: surely God is good. In verse 13 it states the doubt: surely in vain I have kept my heart pure. In verse 18 it states the resolution: surely You set them on slick ground. The same small word can carry a confident conclusion, a bitter complaint or a corrected vision. The translation 'only' or 'nevertheless' is also possible in verse 1, which turns the opening into a hard-won stance, 'nevertheless God is good.'

The word 'good' frames the psalm. It opens with 'God is good to Israel,' verse 1, and closes with 'it is good to draw near to God,' verse 28. Between them the psalmist has moved from confessing that God is good to discovering what the goodness is: not comfort or wealth, but nearness. The psalm ends by relocating the good from the wicked man's table to God's presence.

The middle of the psalm is a study in bodily language. The wicked have well-fed bodies, verse 4, a necklace of pride, verse 6, eyes that bulge with fatness, verse 7, and mouths set against heaven, verse 9. The psalmist, by contrast, has a heart, hands, feet and steps that are struggling. In verse 26 his flesh and heart may fail, but God is his rock and portion. The whole psalm is a contest between two kinds of fullness.

The address changes after the turn. Verses 1 to 16 speak about the wicked and about himself, with only a passing 'Your children' in verse 15, and the sustained 'You' begins in verse 18. Once he is in God's presence he talks to Him. That change of address is one of the quiet marks of the psalm's healing.
context.historical:
Asaph was one of the three Levitical musicians David placed over the worship of the ark, and he was appointed chief, 1 Chronicles 16:4 and 5. His family continued as singers for generations, and Hezekiah's Levites sang 'in the words of David and of Asaph the seer,' 2 Chronicles 29:30. Psalm 73 is the first of eleven Asaph psalms that stand together at the head of Book III, Psalms 73 to 83, and the title may refer to Asaph himself or to a guild of singers that carried his name. Either way the voice is that of a temple singer, a man whose vocation was to praise God, who nearly lost his faith.

That detail sharpens the crisis. The man who leads worship is the one who says the wicked seem to have the better deal. He is also a Levite, and Levites had no land of their own. The LORD was to be their portion, Numbers 18:20 and Deuteronomy 10:9. When he says at the end that God is 'my portion forever,' verse 26, he is using the word of his own tribe's calling. The wicked have estates; the Levite has God, and the psalm is the story of his coming to see that as wealth.

The prosperity described is that of an agrarian and commercial society where the strong could grow rich while the weak went without. The wicked of the psalm 'threaten oppression,' verse 8, and their prosperity is tied to violence and arrogance. The problem is not unique to Israel; Job, Jeremiah 12:1 and 2, Habakkuk 1:13 and Malachi 3:14 and 15 all complain of the same thing in Israel's own literature. Israel's covenant theology promised blessing to the faithful, and experience seemed to say otherwise.

The placement in Book III matters. The Asaph collection speaks repeatedly of national ruin, temple destruction and the silence of God, most notably in Psalms 74, 79 and 80. Psalm 73 reads as the personal doorway into that darker collection: a man tests the doctrine of God's goodness, and the psalms that follow test it on a national scale. Later readers, whether in exile or under foreign rule, would have found in it words for their own struggle.
context.canonical:
The problem of Psalm 73 runs through the wisdom literature and the prophets. Psalm 37 begins, 'Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong,' Psalm 37:1, and answers by promising that the wicked wither like grass, with the striking line, 'the future of the wicked will be cut off,' Psalm 37:38. Psalm 49 asks a very similar question and says that a man in his wealth who has no understanding is 'like the beasts that perish,' Psalm 49:12, and continues, 'But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself,' Psalm 49:15. Psalm 73 shares ground with both, in 'brute beast,' verse 22, and 'receive me,' verse 24.

Job is the most extended treatment. His friends insist that the wicked always suffer; Job answers, 'Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?' Job 21:7. Zophar's description of the wicked flying away 'like a dream' in Job 20:8 resembles verse 20. Job's problem is resolved not by an argument but by a meeting: 'My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You,' Job 42:5. That is the same shape as Psalm 73, where the answer arrives by entering God's presence.

Jeremiah asks it in his own voice, 'Why does the way of the wicked prosper?' Jeremiah 12:1, and Habakkuk asks why God is silent when the wicked swallow those more righteous than themselves, Habakkuk 1:13. Malachi records people saying 'It is futile to serve God,' Malachi 3:14, and then promises that God will keep a scroll of remembrance and that they will again distinguish between righteous and wicked, Malachi 3:16 to 18. The Old Testament never denies the problem. It keeps giving the same answer in different forms: God sees, and the end is not yet.

The New Testament reads the psalm's hope in light of resurrection and the world to come. Jesus, in the story of the rich man and Lazarus, shows the reversal that the psalm sensed, Luke 16:25, and warns, 'Woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort,' Luke 6:24. James warns the wealthy who have oppressed workers, James 5:1 to 6. Paul, facing death, says that to depart and be with Christ is 'far better indeed,' Philippians 1:23, and the phrase echoes 'receive me in glory.' The psalm's cry, 'Whom have I in heaven but You?', belongs to the New Testament's heaven as much as the Old Testament's sanctuary.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Asaph wrote to keep the faith of the people, and specifically of those who were tempted to give up. The psalm is not a cold argument against envy. It is a confession that envy nearly ruined him, and it lets the reader watch how it works: a glance at another man's life, a comparison, a private thought that his own purity is wasted, and a temptation to say so aloud. Asaph wanted his hearers to recognize the sequence in themselves before it took them.

He also meant to show what actually breaks the spell. It is not that the wicked are less comfortable than they seemed, and it is not a new argument. It is entering the sanctuary and seeing things from where God stands. Asaph's authorial purpose is therefore worship: he wanted the people to bring their questions into God's house rather than to leave the house because of them.

A third intention is the correction of the self. Asaph is unusually hard on his former thinking: 'I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You,' verse 22. He wants no one to defend the envy as reasonable. At the same time he never disowns his pain. Both are on the page, and the reader is meant to feel that honest doubt brought to God is quite different from doubt nursed in private.

And he meant the psalm to end in a decision to speak. He did not say his doubts aloud to the people, verse 15, because that would have betrayed the community; he says in verse 28 that he will proclaim all God's works. The psalm is a teacher's testimony, offered to the generation of God's children so that they will not slip as he almost did.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes what the psalmist saw and felt, and much of what he saw is a distorted view. The claim in verses 4 and 12 that the wicked have no struggle and are always carefree is what the psalmist believed before entering the sanctuary. It is an accurate report of his perception, and not a promise that the wicked will always prosper or that they never suffer. The chapter itself corrects it in verses 18 to 20.

Nor does the psalm promise that the righteous will be prosperous. Asaph stays afflicted 'all day long' after his turn, or at least the psalm does not say his affliction ends. What changes is his understanding. The psalm should not be taken as a formula in which faith produces wealth, or as a threat that the wicked will be visibly ruined in this life.

The psalm prescribes a way of handling envy and doubt: do not speak the poison abroad when it would harm others, bring the question into God's presence, wait for his verdict, and finally give the loss its true name. It also prescribes a way of loving God: choosing him as portion and refuge. The believer is not commanded to feel no envy; the psalm assumes that envy comes and shows how it is defeated. This makes the psalm useful to anyone who has ever looked at a rival's success and felt the ground move.

debates.question: What exactly did Asaph 'discern' about the wicked's end upon entering the sanctuary, verse 17?

views.label: Their imminent downfall in this life
views.case: Verses 18 to 20 describe sudden ruin, being swept away by terrors, in the language of historical reversals. Psalm 37:35 and 36 also describes the wicked man who flourished and then 'passed away and was no more.'

views.label: Final judgment beyond this life
views.case: Verse 24 puts Asaph's own being taken 'in glory' beside the wicked's destruction, which implies a reckoning that goes beyond any earthly setback. The 'awakening' of verse 20 also suggests a final day.

debates.bearing: Both fit the text. The sanctuary reveals that the wicked man's security was never real, whether God removes it in this life or at the last day, and it shows that the righteous are secure in God in either case.

debates.question: What does 'later receive me in glory' in verse 24 promise?

views.label: Honor and vindication in this life
views.case: The Hebrew can be taken to mean that God will lead the psalmist afterward to honor, that is, restore his standing. The verse sits between promises of guidance and of being held by the hand, both present-tense blessings.

views.label: Being taken into God's presence after death
views.case: The verb 'receive' is the one used of Enoch, whom God 'had taken away,' Genesis 5:24, and of Elijah, 2 Kings 2:9 and 10, and Psalm 49:15 uses it of God taking the psalmist to Himself out of Sheol. Together with verse 26, 'my flesh and my heart may fail,' the reading toward life after death has strong support.

debates.bearing: Even readers who take the first view should see that the psalm's hope, God as portion forever, cannot end at death. The New Testament makes the second reading explicit, Philippians 1:23, and it fits the psalm's own direction.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 begins with 'ak, and the small word deserves attention because it opens verses 1, 13 and 18. It can mean 'surely' or 'only' or 'nevertheless,' and each shade fits. Read as 'nevertheless,' the first verse is not a placid creed but a stance taken against the evidence: whatever it looks like, God is good to Israel. The same word in verse 13 carries the opposite conclusion, and in verse 18 it settles the matter. One particle carries three moods.

The phrase 'pure in heart' in verse 1 is bare levav, and verse 13 says he kept his heart 'pure' and washed his hands in innocence. Psalm 24:4 asks who may stand in God's holy place, and answers 'He who has clean hands and a pure heart.' Asaph is using the entrance requirement for the sanctuary to complain that his purity was for nothing, and then he enters the sanctuary anyway. The irony is deliberate.

Verse 4 says the wicked 'have no struggle in their death,' where the noun is rare and its meaning uncertain, and the translation 'struggle' is a best guess. Verse 7's Hebrew is literal about their appearance, and the BSB notes, 'Literally Their eye bulges with fatness; Syriac From their callous heart proceeds iniquity.' Verse 10 is the most difficult verse in the psalm, with the BSB footnote 'Or His people.' Both notes are reminders that some of the psalm's descriptive phrases are hard, and that the argument does not rest on any single uncertain word.

In verse 17 the word translated 'sanctuary' is plural in Hebrew, and it is often taken as a plural of majesty for the holy place, though some suggest a reference to the sanctuary's rooms or courts. He 'discerned' their end, from the verb bin, to understand. The noun he understood is acharit, the end or the future, the word used in Psalm 37:38 and Proverbs 23:18 for what waits beyond the present. The psalm turns on seeing an acharit that the eye alone could not see.

Verse 20 says God will 'despise their form,' and the noun is tselem, the word for 'image' in Genesis 1:26. Here it means something like a phantom or a mere semblance, as in Psalm 39:6, where every man goes about like a phantom. The word that names humanity's dignity as God's image is used, in a bitter irony, of the wicked's hollow show. When God wakes, the insubstantial outline they made of themselves disappears like a dream.

Verse 21 says his heart was 'grieved' and he was 'pierced within,' language built on souring and pricking, an embittered heart and stinging kidneys, which in Hebrew thought were the seat of the deepest feelings. In verse 22 he calls himself a behemoth, an intensive plural for a beast, and 'senseless,' an old word for the brutish person who cannot grasp what God is doing, as in Psalm 92:6.

Verse 23 says 'You hold my right hand,' with the verb achaz, to seize or grasp. It is the language of a guide who grips a stumbling child, and it inverts the opening of the psalm, where the man's own feet were slipping. Isaiah 41:13 has the same picture of God taking hold of His servant's right hand.

In verse 26 the BSB says God is 'the strength of my heart,' with the footnote 'Hebrew rock.' The noun is tsur, the rock of refuge, and this is why the psalm belongs with Psalm 71:3. The word for portion, cheleq, is the Levite's word for what they were given in place of land. The verb for 'fail' in verse 26, kalah, is the same as in Psalm 71:9 and Psalm 84:2, where the soul faints for God's courts. Failing bodies and fainting hearts are here folded into God's steadiness.

Verse 27 calls the perishing 'unfaithful,' from zanah, the verb for adultery. Their fault is not merely wickedness but broken covenant love.

typology.type: The sanctuary where the truth is seen, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: Asaph enters God's sanctuary and sees rightly. The tabernacle and temple were the places where God met His people, a picture of access under limits. Hebrews says believers now have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, through the curtain of His body, Hebrews 10:19 and 20, and that Christ has entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in God's presence, Hebrews 9:24. What Asaph needed to reach a building, believers have in a person. The type falls short because the inner rooms of the sanctuary were closed to all but the priests, while in Christ every believer is welcome.

The picture of God gripping the psalmist's right hand is the picture of the shepherd who does not let go. Jesus said of His sheep, 'No one can snatch them out of My hand,' John 10:28, and He literally reached out and took hold of Peter as he sank, Matthew 14:31. The psalm's assurance is embodied in Christ's nail-scarred hands. The type falls short because the psalmist's hold came by a poetic confession, while ours is secured by what Christ has done.

typology.type: Received in glory and God as portion forever, verses 24 and 26
typology.fulfillment: Asaph's hope that God will take him into glory anticipates the destiny of those in Christ. Paul says that when Christ, who is our life, appears, 'then you also will appear with Him in glory,' Colossians 3:4, and that to depart and be with Christ is far better, Philippians 1:23. Peter speaks of an inheritance 'that can never perish, spoil, or fade,' 1 Peter 1:4. The psalm's portion forever is a Levite's hope; in Christ it becomes the hope of every believer, and it rests on His resurrection. The type falls short in that Asaph could see the destination only dimly.

typology.type: The righteous sufferer who kept his heart pure, verses 13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: Asaph complains that he kept his heart pure and yet is afflicted all day long. Only one person could say this without exaggeration. Jesus alone had done no violence and no deceit was in His mouth, Isaiah 53:9, and He was afflicted and rejected. Where Asaph's complaint was tinged with self-pity, Christ suffered in innocence and for others. The type falls short because Asaph's claim to purity was partial, while Christ's was total.

study.christ:
Psalm 73 leads to Christ by the way it ends, with a man whose whole good is God. 'Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You,' verse 25. The New Testament shows this as more than a poet's mood. Paul counts everything as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ, Philippians 3:8, and the writer of Hebrews tells us to look to Jesus, Hebrews 12:2. Christ is the one in whom the psalm's 'portion forever' becomes concrete: He is the inheritance Peter describes, an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade, 1 Peter 1:4.

The psalm leads to Christ through the theme of the sanctuary. The turning point is entering God's presence and seeing things as they are. Hebrews says that this is now open to every believer, because Jesus has opened a new and living way through the curtain, which is His body, Hebrews 10:19 and 20. The wisdom that Asaph needed on a dark night is available to anyone who draws near to the Father through the Son. When Jesus says, 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God,' Matthew 5:8, He speaks the language of Psalm 73:1 and answers Asaph's worry that purity is wasted: it is the very thing that leads to seeing God.

It leads to Christ by contrast with the rich fool and the rich man. Jesus tells of a man whose ground produced abundantly and who said to himself, 'Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry,' Luke 12:16 to 20, and of a rich man who feasted every day while a beggar lay at his door, Luke 16:19 to 25. In each the sudden overthrow of the prosperous, 'How suddenly they are laid waste,' verse 19, is played out. Jesus asks, 'What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?', Matthew 16:26. The psalm's question about prosperity and its end is answered in His teaching.

It also leads to Christ by a better sufferer. Asaph says he was afflicted all day long and punished every morning, verse 14, though he protests it was undeserved. Christ actually was innocent, and His sufferings were not the price of his own sin but of ours. Where Asaph is tempted to conclude that faithfulness does not pay, Christ went further into affliction than any other person and came out into resurrection, and His resurrection proves that the innocence which suffers is not in vain.

Finally, the psalm's hope of being received in glory finds its ground in Christ. 'I go to prepare a place for you,' He says, 'and I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am,' John 14:2 and 3. The Hebrew hope that God would take Asaph to Himself is, in the gospel, a promise from the One who has gone before. Paul can therefore say that nothing, not death nor life, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:38 and 39. Asaph's 'my flesh and my heart may fail' finds its full answer: they fail, and Christ does not.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm does not name a Messiah, and nothing in it demands to be read as a direct prophecy of Jesus' life. The links are by theme, pattern and the New Testament's own use of its language, especially the sanctuary, the portion and the glory.
study.god:
Psalm 73 puts the doctrine of God under the heaviest test it can bear: what if the good do not visibly prosper? The psalm's answer begins with God's goodness as a fixed point. It is the opening line of the psalm, 'Surely God is good to Israel,' and it is the closing line in another form, 'it is good to draw near to God.' The psalmist never doubts it as a proposition. What he discovers is what goodness means. God's goodness is not the same as the distribution of wealth in the present age.

The psalm shows a God who sees. The wicked say, 'How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?', verse 11, and the psalm answers that He knows their end, verse 17, that He 'awakens' and despises their form, verse 20, and that He knows the heart of the man who prays. The God who sees does not miss the pure hands and the afflicted heart of the faithful, and He does not miss the arrogance of those who deny Him. Omniscience is here not an abstract attribute but a comfort to the one who is watched by no one else.

He is a God of justice who acts at His own time. Verses 18 to 20 speak of ruin that is sudden and complete. The wicked live on slick ground, and God is the one who sets them there. Yet the psalm does not tell when the fall comes, and the whole point of the turn is that the psalmist learns to stop needing to see it. God's justice does not depend on the timing that envy requires.

He is a God who holds. 'You hold my right hand,' verse 23. The whole crisis was described in terms of Asaph's feet, but the rescue is described in terms of God's hand. The psalm never says that Asaph hangs on. He says that God has taken hold of him, and he was held even in the worst of his doubt. God does not wait for a man to recover his faith before He holds him, since verse 23 comes right after the confession 'I was a brute beast before You.'

He is a God who guides and who receives. 'You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory,' verse 24. The verbs suggest a whole life: guided now, taken up at the end. This is God as the traveler's companion, who accompanies through the journey and does not abandon at its end.

He is the sufficient God. 'God is the strength of my heart,' or, as the footnote says, the rock of my heart, 'and my portion forever,' verse 26. The psalm claims that God alone can satisfy in heaven and on earth, and this is the strongest claim about His worth in the psalm.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to bring our worst thoughts into God's presence, not to hide them. It shows that God is patient with honest confusion and does not require us to have finished the argument before we come. It invites us to place our envy beside His goodness, our fear beside His hand, and to see the shape of life from the sanctuary. And it ends with the resolve to tell of His works, so that praise becomes the fruit of the struggle.

crossReferences.note: Psalm 37 begins 'Do not fret over those who do evil' and looks at the wicked man who flourished and then was gone. Its 'future of the wicked will be cut off' matches Asaph's discovery of their end. The two psalms address the same problem, one as advice and the other as testimony.

This psalm contrasts the self-confident rich, who are like the beasts that perish and go down to Sheol, with the psalmist whom God will redeem and take to Himself. The verb 'take' is the one used in Psalm 73:24 for being received. The two psalms are companions on the hope of life beyond death.

Job asks why the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power, with safe homes and no rod of punishment. It describes the observation that Asaph makes in verses 4 to 12, and shows the problem was known long before and was not a sign of weak faith.

Jeremiah puts the question to God in prayer: why does the way of the wicked prosper, and why do the faithless live at ease? He notes that God is ever on their lips but far from their hearts. It is close to Asaph's complaint, and it is an example that the prophet, too, was permitted to ask.

The people say it is futile to serve God and that the arrogant are blessed. God answers with a scroll of remembrance for those who fear Him and the promise that they will again distinguish between the righteous and the wicked. It is the same answer as Psalm 73, that the accounts are not closed.

The question 'Who may ascend the hill of the LORD?' is answered with clean hands and a pure heart. Asaph draws on this language in verses 1 and 13. His complaint that his purity has done nothing is thus set against the entrance liturgy, and his entry into the sanctuary answers it.

God tells Aaron that he will have no inheritance in the land, but 'I am your portion and your inheritance.' Asaph was a Levite, and his confession that God is his portion forever is the tribe's calling made personal.

Psalm 71 calls God a rock of refuge and fortress, and Psalm 73:26 calls Him the rock of the psalmist's heart, as the footnote shows. Read together, the neighboring psalms give an aged man and a doubting worshiper the same steadying image.

God takes hold of His servant's right hand and says 'Do not fear, I will help you.' The promise gives the language of Psalm 73:23 a wider setting, and it shows that being held by God is His characteristic way with His people.

Paul weighs living and dying and says that departing to be with Christ is far better. It reads like the New Testament's clear form of Psalm 73:24 and 25, where the man who has God as his portion is not afraid of death.

Believers can enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, through the curtain of His body, with a true heart in full assurance of faith. The sanctuary where Asaph found clarity is now approached through Christ.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 73 gives one of the Bible's frankest answers to a question that arises from the fall. God made a world that was very good, and Genesis 3 explains why it no longer looks that way. Since then the righteous have suffered and the proud have thrived, and the story of Scripture is partly the story of God's people learning to live with that fact without giving up on Him. Cain's line builds a city while Abel lies dead, Genesis 4. The wicked in Babel build a tower, and Israel's prophets spend centuries asking why the way of the wicked prospers.

The psalm answers not with a theory but with a place. God's dwelling among His people is the answer to the whole problem, because His presence is where the true measure of things appears. Eden was the first sanctuary, where God walked with man, and Israel's tabernacle and temple were pictures of the way back. The pattern of the Bible is that people who see God rightly see all else rightly. Isaiah went into the temple in the year King Uzziah died and saw the Lord, and the entire situation looked different, Isaiah 6:1. Asaph does the same.

The psalm also carries forward the hope of a life that death does not end. The Old Testament intimates this in Enoch and Elijah, who were taken, in Psalm 49:15, and in Psalm 73:24. It is not yet fully clear, and Asaph is reaching. The New Testament makes it clear in the resurrection of Jesus, who has gone ahead as forerunner, Hebrews 6:19 and 20. The believer's portion is not exhausted by this life. Whatever the wicked have gained, they will lose, and whatever the righteous have lost, they will find again.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, the truly pure of heart who was truly afflicted, and who through suffering entered glory. He is the portion of His people and the rock of their heart, and He holds them so that no one can snatch them from His hand, John 10:28. His ascension is the shape of Asaph's hope: God receives one of His own in glory, and He brings others after Him.

At the end of the story, the prosperity of the wicked is finally exposed. In Revelation, the great city that had made so many rich is destroyed 'in a single hour,' Revelation 18:17 and 19, an echo of the psalm's 'How suddenly they are laid waste.' Those who trusted in God receive what they had hoped for: God Himself dwells with them, they see His face, and He wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:3 and 4, Revelation 22:4. The one who once said 'It is good to draw near to God' will find that nearness has become the whole of life.

sermon.title: Battling the Unbelief of Despondency
sermon.why: Preached from Psalm 73:21-26, Piper works through Asaph's failing flesh and heart to show that unbelief, not circumstance alone, is the root of yielding to despondency, and that God remains the strength of the heart even when it fails.

quiz.q: What nearly caused Asaph's feet to stumble, verses 2-3?

options.text: Envying the arrogant when he saw the prosperity of the wicked.
options.note: This is the psalm's opening confession and the crisis it wrestles with throughout.

options.text: A physical illness that weakened his body.
options.note: His crisis was one of faith and perspective, not primarily physical illness.

options.text: Being exiled from Jerusalem.
options.note: The text does not mention exile; the crisis is envy over the wicked's ease.

options.text: Losing an argument with a false prophet.
options.note: No such argument is described; the struggle is internal envy and doubt.

quiz.q: What finally changed Asaph's perspective on the wicked's prosperity, verse 17?

options.text: Entering God's sanctuary, where he discerned their end.
options.note: This is the psalm's decisive turning point, resolving the crisis through nearness to God rather than argument alone.

options.text: Reading a letter from a friend.
options.note: No such letter appears; the turning point is entering the sanctuary.

options.text: Winning a great military victory.
options.note: The psalm describes no battle; the resolution is spiritual and comes through God's presence.

options.text: Simply forgetting about the wicked entirely.
options.note: He does not merely forget them; he gains a clear-eyed view of their true, fragile end.

quiz.q: What does Asaph discover about the ground the wicked stand on, verse 18?

options.text: It is slick, slippery ground on which God will cast them down into ruin.
options.note: Their apparent security proves treacherous and unstable once seen from the sanctuary.

options.text: It is the most secure and fertile land in Israel.
options.note: The opposite; their standing is revealed as precarious, not secure.

options.text: It belongs rightfully to them forever.
options.note: The psalm reveals their standing to be temporary and unstable, not a lasting possession.

options.text: It is protected by their own wealth.
options.note: Their wealth does not protect them; God Himself sets them on unstable ground.

quiz.q: What confession does Asaph make in verse 26 about his own weakness?

options.text: "My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever."
options.note: This is the psalm's central confession of confidence beyond physical and emotional collapse.

options.text: "My flesh and heart are stronger than any trouble."
options.note: He openly admits his flesh and heart may fail; his hope rests in God, not his own strength.

options.text: "I no longer need God now that I am wise."
options.note: The opposite; his confidence deepens in dependence on God, not independence from Him.

options.text: "I will seek my portion in wealth like the wicked."
options.note: He explicitly rejects this path, having learned that God alone, not wealth, is his true portion.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's resolution connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Paul similarly counts all things as loss compared to knowing Christ, echoing 'whom have I in heaven but You,' Philippians 3:8.
options.note: Asaph's confession anticipates the surpassing worth believers find in Christ alone.

options.text: It predicts the exact wealth Solomon would accumulate.
options.note: The psalm makes no such prediction; its focus is Asaph's own crisis of faith.

options.text: It has no connection to New Testament teaching.
options.note: Its language and resolution are directly echoed in passages like Philippians 3 and 1 Peter 1.

options.text: It teaches that wealth is always sinful.
options.note: The psalm critiques wicked arrogance fueled by wealth, not wealth itself as inherently sinful.

questions: Asaph nearly stumbled from envying the carefree prosperity of the arrogant, verses 2-3. Whose apparent ease or success tempts you most to doubt God's goodness?

His crisis was resolved not by winning an argument but by entering God's sanctuary, verse 17. What would it look like this week to bring your hardest doubts into God's presence rather than trying to reason your way out alone?
Asaph discovers the wicked stand on ground that only looks secure, verse 18. Where in your own life have you mistaken something fragile for something solid?
He confesses that God is the strength of his heart even when flesh and heart fail, verse 26. What losses or weaknesses in your life most need this confession right now?

Asaph concludes it is good to draw near to God and make Him his refuge, verse 28. What single step could you take today to draw nearer to God rather than nearer to the things that only seem to offer security?

translationNotes.note: The phrase rendered 'from their prosperity proceeds iniquity' is literally 'their eye bulges with fatness' in Hebrew, a vivid picture of gross, self-satisfied excess; some ancient versions read instead 'from their callous heart proceeds iniquity.'
'Their people' can also be rendered 'his people,' a small textual ambiguity that does not change the picture of a crowd drawn to and swayed by the wicked's apparent success.
'The strength of my heart' translates a Hebrew word literally meaning 'rock,' the same image used elsewhere in the Psalms for God as an unmoving foundation when every other support gives way.
